summary: Citizens of around 100 visa-exempt countries — including the EU, US, UK, Canada and Australia — can visit Israel for up to 90 days but must obtain an ETA-IL electronic travel authorization before boarding; other nationalities need a B/2 visitor visa from an Israeli consulate.

primarySources.name: ETA-IL — Israel Population and Immigration Authority: Learn about ETA-IL

AF.notes: Israel's Foreign Ministry lists Afghanistan as requiring a tourist visa for national, diplomatic and service passports, with a fee for national passports; Afghan passport holders are not eligible for an ETA-IL. The Population and Immigration Authority says B/2 tourist and visitor visa applications are submitted in person at Israeli missions abroad, or by an Israeli citizen or resident inviting the visitor at its offices in Israel, and that applicants from countries the security services define as "high-risk" must add a resume form for security clearance (the countries are not named).

defaultStayWindow.text: The Population and Immigration Authority states that an approved ETA-IL lets you “stay for up to 90 days per visit”. The authority does not say whether the days of arrival and departure are counted, so we count both.

fee.notes: Per traveler, paid online; the Population and Immigration Authority says it cannot be refunded after you apply.

fee.notes: The Foreign Ministry's 2026 consular tariff for a B/2 visitor visa at Israeli missions: USD 32 or €28, charged in local currency. Indian and Sri Lankan passport holders living in India or Sri Lanka can instead apply online through the eVisa-B2 pilot, for a 105 NIS handling fee.

currencyLimits.text: Cash and other means of payment (bank and travellers' cheques, bearer securities, negotiable instruments, payment cards) worth ILS 50,000 or more must be declared on entry and exit at any border crossing, and ILS 12,000 or more at the Nizana, Jordan River, Yitzhak Rabin, Taba and Allenby land crossings. At Allenby the declaration is made through a separate online service.

tips.text: The UK FCDO says visitors arriving at Ben Gurion Airport get an entry card instead of a passport stamp; at other entry points you may get a card or a stamp. Keep the card with your passport until you leave — it is evidence that you entered legally, and you may need it if you cross into Palestine.

The UK FCDO lists three land crossings with Jordan — Allenby/King Hussein Bridge, the northern Jordan River/Sheikh Hussein crossing and the southern Yitzhak Rabin/Wadi Araba crossing — and says they may be restricted or closed at short notice. Check the Israel Airports Authority's updates before you go.
The UK FCDO says you may face lengthy personal questioning and baggage searches at security when you enter and leave Israel.
The UK FCDO says Shabbat runs from sunset on Friday to nightfall on Saturday, and advises against driving into ultra-Orthodox areas of Jerusalem on Shabbat, where residents may throw stones at cars.

faq.question: Do I need a visa for Israel?
faq.answer: If you are from one of the roughly 100 visa-exempt countries — the EU, US, UK, Canada, Australia, most of Latin America and others — you do not need a visa for stays of up to 90 days, but you must obtain an ETA-IL electronic travel authorization online before boarding. Most other nationalities need a B/2 visitor visa from an Israeli embassy or consulate; the Foreign Ministry lists, among others, Afghan, Lebanese, Libyan, Pakistani, Saudi, Somali, Sudanese, Syrian and Yemeni passports as needing a tourist visa.

faq.question: What is ETA-IL and how do I get one?
faq.answer: ETA-IL is Israel's electronic travel authorization, mandatory for visa-exempt visitors. Apply at israel-entry.piba.gov.il with your passport details; the fee is ILS 25 per traveler. It is valid for two years (or until your passport expires) and covers multiple visits of up to 90 days.

faq.question: Does Israel stamp your passport?
faq.answer: Not at Ben Gurion Airport: the UK FCDO says visitors arriving there get an entry card instead of a passport stamp, while at other entry points you may get either a card or a stamp. The FCDO's advice for Iran says stamps from other countries' border crossings with Israel can also lead to refusal of entry there.

faq.question: Will visiting Israel prevent me from entering other countries?
faq.answer: The UK FCDO says an Israeli stamp or other evidence of travel to Israel may get you refused entry to Iran, Lebanon, Syria and Kuwait — for Iran this includes stamps from other countries' border crossings with Israel — and that a passport showing previous travel to Israel will not be accepted for travel to Libya. It also says visitors entering through Ben Gurion Airport get an entry card instead of a passport stamp.

faq.question: Is it safe to visit Israel right now?
faq.answer: The UK FCDO advises against all travel to Gaza and within 500 m of the border with Gaza, and to parts of northern Israel and the occupied Golan Heights, and says rocket fire can affect most areas of Israel; it tells travellers to check Home Front Command for the latest guidance. Australia's Smartraveller advises reconsidering the need to travel to Israel and not travelling to the border areas with Gaza, Lebanon and Syria.
